prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single prize part on B043 naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. All six round-1 files reached the same configuration, but I do not treat that as evidence. The scientific case stands on its own: an unbroken line from proglucagon processing and the human incretin effect (Holst, Drucker), through identification of the biologically active peptide (Mojsov), to therapies with large, independently confirmed outcome benefits in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is stable, the discovery is mature without being exhausted, and recognition is timely. I see no case for a second prize part: the three-person limit means a second part would force Mojsov or another core name out, and none of the alternatives is clean enough on credit to justify that cost.
statement.case_against: The third slot is a judgement call, not a settled fact. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited, and the supplied evidence cannot resolve it. Leaving out Knudsen, who designed liraglutide and semaglutide, means the prize honours the physiology and the identification of the peptide but not the step that made it a medicine. The committee must be willing to say openly that this omission is deliberate and defensible, not costless. If the primary-literature record were shown to weaken Mojsov's claim materially, Knudsen would become the natural third name and the citation should then be reframed around the therapies.

responses.point: The Nobel question is the discovery, and analogue design builds on a discovery already made; a Knudsen prize would read as recognition of one company's drug programme, though Knudsen becomes the natural third name if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended.
responses.response: I agree with the principle, and it is the reason I moved away from my opening ballot, where I credited Knudsen. Your conditional is the right test: the decision turns on whether Mojsov's priority can be defended, not on how impressive the drugs are. I am not persuaded that the unresolved Habener dispute alone removes her, because on the supplied evidence it has not been shown that her identification of the active truncated form is secondary. I differ slightly in that I would not call the analogue work merely derivative. It is a separate, major achievement, and the committee should say in its deliberation that this prize does not diminish it.

responses.point: If the citation is framed around the therapies, Knudsen would not be opposed, but the committee must then explain why Mojsov, and not Knudsen, is the name left out; also GLP-1 may be almost too obvious and should not displace the overdue unfolded protein response (B032).
responses.response: Your symmetry argument is fair and I accept it: whichever name is left out needs an explanation that does not depend on the other. My explanation is that the citation is built on physiology and the active peptide, so Mojsov is inside it and Knudsen is outside it by design. On B032, I still think it is among the strongest basic-science cases and keep it as my first alternative. But being obvious is not a scientific objection to GLP-1, and the question of what disease-level evidence would let UPR modulation compete with a mature therapeutic line has not been answered in this exchange. The credit record for B032 is also less tidy than the two-name pairing implies, given Ron, Kaufman and the PERK, ATF6 and integrated stress response arms. So I do not see a reason to split the prize or to rank B032 ahead of B043 this year.

responses.point: Keep Mojsov over Knudsen unless the priority evidence against her is stronger than the opening ballots suggest; the contested nature of Mojsov's credit is the argument that most moves you towards a Knudsen configuration.
responses.response: I take the same view of the evidence: neither of us can adjudicate the Habener dispute from the supplied text. Where I land is that contested priority is a reason for care in wording, not for exclusion. I would therefore support a citation that says 'identification of its active form' with precision and does not claim more than the record supports. If a member could point to primary-literature evidence, for instance dated sequence and activity data, that Mojsov's contribution to the active form was secondary, I would change my position. Absent that, my disclosed co-authorship with you plays no role, since neither of us is credited on any shortlisted ballot.

responses.point: A basic-science-centred GLP-1 prize would more naturally name Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and omit the industrial developer Knudsen, but the omission should be stated openly.
responses.response: I agree on the configuration and on openness about the omission. In round 1 I conceded that the omission should be noted, and I now think the citation can do that without naming Knudsen, by stating that the discoveries 'enabled' therapies rather than claiming the therapies themselves. That keeps the prize on the discovery while telling the reader why the drugs are not the prize. I would not go further and add Knudsen's name to the citation text, since that would amount to a four-name credit through the back door.

responses.point: If GLP-1 is awarded, CAR-T or cGAS-STING should be the candidate held for a later year, given attribution and maturity.
responses.response: On the question of which of B032, B019 and B013 to hold, I rank them slightly differently from you. cGAS-STING (B013) is mechanistically elegant and your interferon expertise is relevant, but it carries five credited names and is still early in therapeutic translation, so I place it behind CAR-T and UPR. CAR-T has a clearly demonstrated clinical effect, but Eshhar lies outside the credited names, which is a serious attribution gap. B032 has the cleaner two-name pairing but the weaker clinical consequence. I keep B032 and B019 as my two alternatives and treat the order between them as open, depending on whether the committee can resolve the Eshhar question.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide against Habener's group can be defended, which the supplied evidence does not settle and which would decide the third slot.
Whether the omission of Knudsen is read as an incomplete account of a discovery whose importance rests on therapy, even when stated openly.
Whether a two-part prize pairing B043 with B032 or B019 would be better than a single GLP-1 part; I judge not, under the three-person limit, but members who value B032's overdue status may disagree.
Which of B019, B032 and B013 deserves to be held for a later year, which depends on attribution (Eshhar for B019, Ron and Kaufman for B032) and on clinical consequence that is still developing.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict specific to the shortlisted candidates is apparent. I worked as a postdoctoral fellow with Paul Greengard, and I have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann; neither is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. I disclose both for transparency, and neither requires recusal. Shared Karolinska affiliation with other members is not treated as a conflict.
